topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Debugging is an evidence-gathering process. A debugger can show where a program stopped, what values it currently holds, and how execution reached that point, but those observations still require a hypothesis about the intended contract. This chapter supplies a small deterministic calculation with named stages and a debugger command file so the investigation can be repeated without an intentional crash.

topics.title: 9.1.1 Setting Breakpoints and Watchpoints
topics.summary: A breakpoint stops execution at a function, source location, or condition. A watchpoint observes changes to a selected memory location, subject to debugger and hardware limits. Use them to test a hypothesis: where does this value first violate its bound, or which caller supplies an unexpected argument?

topics.title: 9.1.2 Inspecting Variables and Stack Frames
topics.summary: A stack trace identifies active calls as reconstructed by the debugger. Select a frame to inspect its parameters and locals in that frame’s context. A pointer’s numeric value is only a starting point; establish the pointee’s type, lifetime, and valid extent before treating memory as a meaningful object.

topics.title: 9.2.1 Reading Stack Traces
topics.summary: A trace shows the path active at failure, not necessarily the operation that first corrupted state. A crash in a library allocator may have been caused by an earlier overwrite. Follow the invalid state backward through ownership and recent changes rather than declaring the top frame the root cause.

blocks.text: Capturing and Inspecting a Core Dump from a Controlled Crash
rich: Capturing and Inspecting a Core Dump from a Controlled Crash
blocks.headingContext: Capturing and Inspecting a Core Dump from a Controlled Crash

blocks.text: Purpose
rich: Purpose

blocks.text: Postmortem debugging preserves process state after a crash so the failure can be analyzed without reproducing it under an interactive debugger first.
rich: Postmortem debugging preserves process state after a crash so the failure can be analyzed without reproducing it under an interactive debugger first.

blocks.text: Code or command
rich: Code or command

blocks.text:
ulimit -c unlimited
./crash || true
coredumpctl list ./crash 2>/dev/null || ls -1 core* 2>/dev/null
gdb ./crash core
(gdb) bt
(gdb) frame 0
(gdb) info locals

blocks.text: What the important parts do
rich: What the important parts do

blocks.text: `ulimit` permits core generation where policy allows it. GDB needs the exact executable plus matching core image to resolve addresses into frames and variables; systemd systems may store cores through `coredumpctl` instead of the current directory.
